pr_title: Add default icons for the default profiles
pr_body:
This pull request introduces a handful of default icons whose paths will be
emitted into the default profiles.

Icons are named after the profile GUIDs, which for the default profiles
are stable v5 UUIDs based on the name of the profile. The plan is that
we'll never have a duplicate default profile, and if the user wants to
duplicate it they'll need to issue it a new GUID. Icons will _by default_
be unique for each profile (when the user saves their settings), but they
can of course be shared. It's just a file path.

Eventually, when icons can be inserted through the settings UI, we can
keep the GUID name (to unique them among all icons for all profiles) and
move them into ms-appdata:///roaming/.

The currently included icons are named for the following profiles:

"cmd" `{0caa0dad-35be-5f56-a8ff-afceeeaa6101}`
"PowerShell Core" `{574e775e-4f2a-5b96-ac1e-a2962a402336}`
"Windows PowerShell" `{61c54bbd-c2c6-5271-96e7-009a87ff44bf}`
"WSL" `{9acb9455-ca41-5af7-950f-6bca1bc9722f}`

The PowerShell profile names aren't being used yet, but this is in
preparation for #918 merging.

Fixes #933.

## PR Checklist
* [x] Closes #933
* [x] CLA signed
* [x] Tests added/passed/not required
* [x] Documentation updated/not required
* [x] I've discussed this with core contributors already.
pr_comments: Assets have been signed off for inclusion in Windows and Windows products. The black PowerShell Core icon is used in accordance with the PowerShell assets license described [in this directory](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/tree/master/assets).

Should ` void SetIconPath(std::wstring_view path) noexcept`. 

>https://abseil.io/docs/cpp/guides/strings
>string_view objects are very lightweight, so you should always pass them by value within your methods and functions; don’t pass a const absl::string_view &. (Passing absl::string_view instead of const absl::string_view & has the same algorithmic complexity, but because of register allocation and parameter passing rules, it is generally faster to pass by value in this case.)

`const std::wstring_view &`：
```asm
movq	(%rdi), %rax
```

`std::wstring_view`:
```asm
movq	%rdi, %rax
```
I did not know that, that's fascinating. @adiviness would be interested also
@fcharlie thanks for the info! that's really good to know.
I wonder if CppCoreChecks or linting could catch this...

Sidenote that this seems to match the advice in the ISO C++ guidelines:
[F.16: For “in” parameters, pass cheaply-copied types by value and others by reference to const](https://isocpp.github.io/CppCoreGuidelines/CppCoreGuidelines.html#f16-for-in-parameters-pass-cheaply-copied-types-by-value-and-others-by-reference-to-const)

Key points are:
> What is “cheap to copy” depends on the machine architecture, but two or three words (doubles, pointers, references) are usually best passed by value. When copying is cheap, nothing beats the simplicity and safety of copying, and for small objects (up to two or three words) it is also faster than passing by reference because it does not require an extra indirection to access from the function.

However, using by value instead of by const reference is only appropriate because string_view (data()) is readonly.  const& is preferred when declaring read-only intent or when there's a question around lifetime management.

Is there a difference between `std::wstring_view` and `const std::wstring_view`? I realize that the string views are read only but I'm curious if the compiler is aware enough to take advantage of it if possible.
There's an argument for using const by-value string views (in that the data pointer is made `const` as well)

The std::string_view's data pointer is [always const](https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/string/basic_string_view/data):
`constexpr const_pointer data() const noexcept;`

> Is there a difference between `std::wstring_view` and `const std::wstring_view`? I realize that the string views are read only but I'm curious if the compiler is aware enough to take advantage of it if possible.

In general, compilers don't usually take advantage of const, per LLVM's Chandler Carruth.  This is covered in Chandler's [LLVM Optimization talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FnGCDLhaxKU) (don't have exact timestamp).

const is really more about correctness than optimization.  With that said, I don't know specifically about msvc, but I doubt it.

Since the pointer returned by .data() is always const anyway (see my other comment), the only thing it really does is prevent the callee from manipulating the length which if you're passing by value, doesn't matter.
